name: Eastern Low German
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Lindow et al. 1998, Niederdeutsche Grammatik (Verlag Schuster Leer) plausibly covers stress; not online. Glottolog refs (Wiesinger 1983, Niebaum 2008) are subclassification only

new_statements.quote: Einige der hier erläuterten lautlichen Merkmale lassen sich auf den Wortakzent zurückführen. Die Probanden betonen zumeist stark auf der Stammsilbe. [...] Bei einigen Wörtern weicht die Position des Wortakzents von dem in der Standardsprache ab, so sprechen viele Probanden „Bürgeméister“ (u. a. in Brudersdorf), betonen also auf dem Grundwort, und „Améisn“ (z. B. in Sukow) [...] [Fn. 1500:] Für das vorpommersche Wolgast gibt Warnkross, S. 10, an, „[d]er auf die Stammsilbe einfacher Wörter gerichtete Hauptton ist in unserer Mundart besonders stark. [...] Bei Kompositis trägt die erste Stammsilbe ebenfalls den Starkton, die zweite nur dann, wenn das Wort noch als Kompositum empfunden wird.“
new_statements.translation: Some of the phonetic features explained here can be traced back to word accent. The informants for the most part stress the stem syllable strongly. [...] In some words the position of the word accent differs from that of the standard language: many informants say „Bürgeméister“ (e.g. in Brudersdorf), i.e. they stress the head noun, and „Améisn“ (e.g. in Sukow) [...] [Fn. 1500:] For Wolgast in Western Pomerania Warnkross (p. 10) states: 'the main stress, directed at the stem syllable of simple words, is particularly strong in our dialect. [...] In compounds the first stem syllable likewise carries the strong stress, the second only when the word is still felt to be a compound.'
new_statements.citation: Köhncke, André. 2010/2011. Mecklenburgisch heute – Bestandsaufnahme eines niederdeutschen Dialektes. Inauguraldissertation, Universität Rostock (defended 6 Dec 2010; urn:nbn:de:gbv:28-diss2011-0137-3), 659 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 271 (pdf p. 273), end of the Lautlehre chapter, with footnote 1500 quoting Warnkross 1912: 10 (Wolgast)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Germanic stem-initial stress: the primary stress falls on the (first syllable of the) lexical stem; prefixes are unstressed and reduced (vesábm), suffixes/derivational syllables are weak, and in compounds the first stem carries the main stress. Corroborated first-hand for Brandenburgisch by Mackel 1905: 87 (Prignitz: 'Die Tendenz des Deutschen, die Stammsilbe zu betonen... ist in unserer Mundart stark ausgeprägt') and for Low German generally incl. Stavenhagen/Mecklenburg by Grimme 1922: 17 ('Der stärkste Ton ruht im Plattdeutschen... auf den Stammsilben'). Not strictly fixed-initial because prefixed words and loans are stressed on the stem or on a later syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Warnkross 1912 (via Köhncke fn. 1500): second member of a compound keeps a strong stress only while the word is still felt as a compound. Grimme 1922: 17-18: all derivational syllables strikingly weak; syllables with old secondary stress in High German have become weak in Low German. Teuchert 1907 §13 (Neumark): stress is strongly expiratory, the old primary/secondary distinction is given up, only stressed vs unstressed remains.
new_statements.exceptions: Loans and some compounds deviate from Standard German placement: Bürgeméister, Améisn, Motór, Meschíen 'Maschine', Mesík 'Musik', Teback, ámesìern; Beckmann (quoted p. 271) notes a shift of stress to the middle of High German loans around Schwerin (Großhérzog, Börgerméister, Rechtsánwalt, Améise), now receding; Sünnǻåmt vs Sǘnnååmt vary between speakers.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Wortakzent'), described from field recordings of Mecklenburg dialect speakers (Probanden, place names in Mecklenburg); Warnkross's formulation distinguishes simple words vs compounds for the Wolgast (Vorpommern) dialect. Köhncke's remark is incidental to the phonetic description (reduction, lenition) rather than a dedicated stress section, and hedged with 'zumeist'.
new_statements.identity_note: Köhncke 2011 describes Mecklenburgisch (Mecklenburgisch-Vorpommersch), which Glottolog Corroborating first-hand statements come from Brandenburgisch varieties (Prignitz: Mackel 1905; Neumark: Teuchert 1907) and from Grimme 1922, whose dialect S is Stavenhagen (Mecklenburg). Glottolog 5.1 lists no child languoids for nort2627, so no finer glottocode applies; note that Glottolog's nort2627 reference list also mixes in North Low Saxon works (Hamburg, Emsland, Nordstrand), which were not used.

sources.citation: Mitzka, Walther. 1920. Ostpreußisches Niederdeutsch nördlich vom Ermland. Deutsche Dialektgeographie (offprint, 190 pp. scan, pp. 107-294 of the DDG volume).
sources.note: §172 'Die Accentgrenze' (pp. 200-201): east of a line through Labiau the sentence melody and word accent become more varied; long vowels in open syllables diphthongise and take falling (circumflex) accent. Sections on 'Vocalismus in nebentonigen und unbetonten Silben'. No statement of where word stress falls.

sources.citation: Mackel, Emil. 1905. Die Mundart der Prignitz. Jahrbuch des Vereins für niederdeutsche Sprachforschung 31: 65-164.
sources.note: §16 (p. 87): 'Die Tendenz des Deutschen, die Stammsilbe zu betonen... ist in unserer Mundart stark ausgeprägt'; this drives open-syllable lengthening, overlength, weakening of vowels in unstressed syllables and in compounds, syncope/apocope; the dialect has no circumflex stress. §21 (p. 88): the stem syllable carries the musical main tone except in questions.

sources.citation: Grimme, Hubert. 1922. Plattdeutsche Mundarten (Sammlung Göschen 461), 2nd ed. Berlin/Leipzig: de Gruyter. 176 pp.
sources.note: §25 'Tonstärke' (pp. 17-18): 'Der stärkste Ton ruht im Plattdeutschen, gleichwie im Hochdeutschen, auf den Stammsilben; alle Ableitungssilben sind auffällig tonschwach'; in D (Heide) and S (Stavenhagen, Mecklenburg) the following syllable is so reduced that stem+ending sounds almost monosyllabic. §26: musical accent has little modulation; in S a level word tone is usual.

sources.citation: Teuchert, Hermann. 1907. Laut- und Flexionslehre der neumärkischen Mundart. Teil I: Einleitung und Vokalismus (Diss. Berlin; = Zeitschrift für deutsche Mundarten 2: 103-155).
sources.note: §13 'Akzent' (ZfdM p. 121; offprint p. 21f.): the dialect lacks any musical accentuation; stress is strongly expiratory, so the old distinction of primary vs secondary stress has been given up and only stressed vs unstressed remains; compound/sentence accent marked with an acute when needed, circumflex = two-peaked rising-falling. No explicit placement rule.
